name: Buenos Aires
summary:
Buenos Aires Province carries the strongest sub-national negative signal in Argentina: the federal human-rights ombudsman's 2016 submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents acts of violence, persecution and harassment by provincial police—or by third parties under police cover—against trans and travesti people during operations in La Plata, Mar del Plata and Esteban Echeverría, carried out under "preventive policing" frameworks. Academic legal analysis (CELS CEDAW shadow report; UNLP/Pensamiento Penal) confirms that after the 2012 Gender Identity Law formally decriminalised trans presence, security forces increased use of drug-law prosecution (devolved to provincial justice in 2005) and street-offence law as the operative instrument for indirect criminalisation of travesti/trans identity—a patterned, state-implicated escalation with impunity.

The deviation from the national score (0.58) is −0.05. No other province has a comparable volume of multi-source, patterned enforcement documentation reaching the UN treaty-body system. The evidence is not a single incident but a documented operational framework (drug-law devolution + anti-narcotics security policy) that measurably increased police persecution of trans women. Protective institutions coexist—the provincial defensoría maintains a 2024 registry-rectification guide and documents discrimination caseloads—but these are resident-facing and do not offset the visitor-facing exposure to arbitrary detention during any police stop.

Compared with Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires (0.55), the Province lacks CABA's tribunal contravencional judicial-oversight structure and anti-discrimination apparatus; its police-judge model under the código de faltas gives less post-detention review. Compared with the silent majority of provinces (national score), the difference is one of documented pattern rather than statutory hostility—no BA law criminalises gender identity, but enforcement practice does the work.

name: Ciudad Autónoma de Buenos Aires
summary:
CABA is simultaneously the most legally protective jurisdiction in Latin America and the site of the country's best-documented urban pattern of police round-ups against travestis and trans women. In September 2024—six months after the unlawful detention of Yhajaira Falcón—uniformed and plain-clothes officers from Comisaría 18 carried out fresh "detentions, arrests and arbitrary identifications" in the Constitución neighbourhood, writing up several under article 81 of the City's Contravention Code and arresting one for lacking documents. Activists characterise it as the third-plus iteration of the same operation in the same barrio, qualifying it as a pattern rather than a single incident.

The deviation from the national score (0.58) is −0.03, partially offset by institutional counterweights that a visitor can actually use: CABA's anti-discrimination law, INADI/defensoría presence, the tribunales contravencionales (judicial rather than police oversight—"stronger guarantees" per the dossier), the Diana Sacayán–Lohana Berkins quota-law administration, and MuMaLa's national femicide/travesticidio registry headquartered in the city. These make CABA the jurisdiction most likely to produce a state response to an incident, which is why it scores above Buenos Aires Province (0.53) despite comparable police-practice exposure.

CABA's own Código Contravencional "cuts both ways": art. 81 is still used to write up trans women, but the procedural guarantees (public defender, judicial hearing within 24 hours, no police judge) reduce detention severity relative to the provincial código-de-faltas model. The national DNU 62/2025 prison-placement decree shifts all units equally and is already priced into the 0.58 anchor.
